newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INTERVIEW-EU subsidies not hurting US farmers.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INTERVIEW-EU subsidies not hurting US farmers.

text.p: U.S. Farm Bureau president Dean Kleckner said European agricultural subsidies have not caused U.S. farmers to lose world market share.

As a result, the Farm Bureau, the biggest farmers group in the U.S., is unlikely to demand the U.S. government take retaliatory measures in the form of subsidies under the Export Enhancement Programme (EEP), Kleckner said in an interview.

The European Union last year reintroduced wheat export subsidies, leading to calls from some U.S. groups for retaliation. Firm wheat prices since then appear to have eased the possibility of a trade war over the issue.
Kleckner, an adviser to U.S. President Bill Clinton, is leading a delegation of U.S. farmers on a fact-finding tour of Australia and New Zealand.
"There are elements in our country, particularly in the meat area, that are pressuring to see EEPs reinstated," Kleckner said.
"At this point, we haven't seen a loss of markets in U.S. wheat and actually prices are fairly good right now," Kleckner said.
But he cautioned that any downturn in agricultural prices would step up pressure on the U.S. government to counter European subsidies through the EEP.
Resumption of the EEP, last used about two years ago, however would raise the question of how effective the action would be in countering the most recent European subsidies.
While the U.S. budget calls for US$500 million in EEP funding, Kleckner said it was doubtful that much money would make it into the programme.
"I don't think that level of funding is likely to hold," Kleckner said.
He said the actual appropriation would probably be on a smaller scale, with some of the funds initially earmarked for EEP eventually re-directed elsewhere inside the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
"We think the likelihood of US$500 million being appropriated is very small," Kleckner said.
European farm subsidies are the result of over-inflated government-guaranteed prices to farmers that have failed to take into account the large crop from the most recent harvest, Kleckner said.
"The Europeans just had a lot of wheat to sell," Kleckner said.
